content: Corncockle (Agrostemma githago), also known as Corn cockle or Corn-cockle, is a slender flowering plant with pink blossoms that is native to European cornfields. During the 19th century, it was a prevalent weed in wheat fields. Its seeds were often unintentionally mixed with harvested wheat seeds and subsequently re-sown in the following planting season. It is highly probable that, until the 20th century, most wheat contained some Corncockle seeds. Today, Corncockle is found in various temperate regions of the world as an introduced species, likely brought along with imported European wheat. It is known to grow across much of the United States, parts of Canada, as well as regions of Australia and New Zealand. In certain parts of Europe, such as the United Kingdom, the plant has become uncommon or localized due to intensive mechanized farming practices. This decline is partly attributed to the increased use of herbicides but is more significantly linked to changes in agricultural patterns. Most wheat is now sown in the autumn as winter wheat and harvested before Corncockle has the opportunity to flower or produce seeds. Corncockle is a rigidly upright plant that can grow up to 1 meter in height and is covered with fine hairs. It has few branches, each of which is topped with a single deep pink to purple flower. The flowers are unscented, measuring 25 to 50 millimeters in diameter, and bloom during the summer months—May to September in the Northern Hemisphere and November to March in the Southern Hemisphere. Each petal features two or three discontinuous black lines. The plant has five narrow, pointed sepals that extend beyond the petals and are fused at the base to form a rigid, ribbed tube with ten ridges. The leaves of Corncockle are pale green, arranged oppositely, and narrowly lanceolate. They are held nearly erect against the stem and measure between 45 and 145 millimeters in length. The seeds are produced in a capsule containing many seeds. All parts of the plant are reported to be toxic. Corncockle can be found in fields, along roadsides, near railway lines, in waste areas, and other disturbed habitats.
